#9197. Reformation Steps Into Home Design With Its First Rug Collection

After years of dressing its customers, Reformation is turning its attention to their homes. The Los Angeles-based fashion brand has partnered with French rugmaker Les Éditions de Tapis on its first rug collection, bringing the distinctive designs found in Reformation’s stores into residential spaces.

Swan Fan Circle Rug and Boa Dress in Ivory. Photography courtesy of Reformation.

Reformation has long incorporated rugs by Les Éditions de Tapis founder Thomas Coccimiglio into its retail interiors. “His craftsmanship is unparalleled,” says Lauren Caris Cohan, Reformation’s chief creative officer. “Every Les Éditions de Tapis piece is a work of art that somehow feels both luxurious and whimsical.”

The rugs’ playful patterns and unexpected details have become part of the shopping experience, prompting customers to ask where they could purchase them. Those requests eventually led the two brands to develop a collection specifically for the home.

Chintz Rug in Baby Blue. Photography courtesy of Reformation.

Working together, Cohan and Coccimiglio developed nine limited-edition, made-to-order designs that combine the decorative traditions of Parisian interiors with a more relaxed Los Angeles sensibility. The resulting collection carries Reformation’s fashion sensibility into the home without simply translating clothing designs into floor coverings.

Delicate palm trees, swans, and other figurative motifs appear against softly colored backgrounds, often surrounded by decorative borders that recall antique textiles. Rather than filling every available inch with pattern, many of the rugs leave generous areas of open space, allowing the individual illustrations to stand out.

Le Classique Rug in Ivory and Naya Knit Dress in Tan Tiger. Photography courtesy of Reformation.

Each rug begins as a hand-drawn design before being hand-knotted by artisans in India and Nepal. The process brings traditional rug-making techniques to designs that feel decidedly contemporary.

For Cohan, the move into interiors is less about entering a new product category than extending the design language Reformation has developed across its stores and clothing collections. “We are very intentional about crafting physical environments that reflect who we are in subtle, delightful ways,” she explains. “Like our clothing, there is a sense of ease and elegance with a wink of humor.”

Grand Chintz Rug in Dark Wine. Photography courtesy of Reformation.

The Reformation x Les Éditions de Tapis collection is available at thereformation.com, with prices starting at $1,000. All nine designs are available exclusively online, with material swatches on display at select Reformation stores.

#9196. Oshinówò Studio tops Lutyens-designed war memorial with glass prism to honour Sierra Leone's Carrier Corps

Photography by Tolu Sanusi / Oshinówò Studio unless stated

The Commonwealth War Graves Commission has unveiled a memorial to the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps in Freetown, Sierra Leone.

Officially opened this weekend, the memorial designed by Oshinówò Studio sits on top of a war memorial designed by British architect Edwin Lutyens in 1931.

While the original memorial honoured soldiers who died in the first world war, it did not include the names of the 946 members of the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps – men enlisted to transport supplies and materials – who also died in the war.

Oshinówò Studio extended the Lutyens-designed, stone memorial by adding a structural glass pyramid etched with the names of the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps men.

“The Freetown Memorial is conceived through a material symbolism that allows it to resonate across cultures and contexts,” said Oshinówò Studio founder Tosin Oshinówò.

“The structure we designed is, in effect, an extension of Sir Edwin Lutyens’ existing monument. By following its tapering geometry, the new monument rises higher, elevating the immense volume of names etched into glass. “

According to Oshinówò, placing the names of the carrier corps men higher than the soldiers was also a symbolic move.

“In this gesture, the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps are symbolically carried by their comrades, reversing the relationship between those who served and those who were served,” she said.

“There is a profound irony in this act: it becomes a fitting expression of gratitude to men whose sacrifice was fundamental to shaping the world we inhabit today.”

Along with the glass pyramid, the memorial also includes a laser beacon that will be illuminated on significant days of remembrance. According to the team, this column of light will be visible from up to five kilometres.

As part of the project, the 1930s memorial was also full restored by stonemasons and bronze specialists from the Commonwealth War Graves Commission.

Recent memorials featured on Dezeen include a “serene and contemplative” memorial to Queen Elizabeth II designed by Foster + Partners and a park in Ethiopia dedicated to the 157 victims of the Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 crash.

Photography by Tolu Sanusi / Oshinówò Studio unless stated

#9195. A New MFA Design Program Prepares Designers for an Evolving Industry

Designers today need to do it all. While honing specialized design skills, they are often required to learn marketing, social media strategy, and more. Today’s professionals need to be able to move fluidly between visual communication, product and service design, entrepreneurship, typography, technology, facilitation, research, and cultural strategy—often on the same day. That’s why programs that are designed to help students integrate these modes of practice are so important. At the School of Visual Arts (SVA) in New York City, a new multidisciplinary MFA design program does exactly that.

“Designers today move between media, disciplines, and contexts,” shares Randy Hunt, current SVA MFA Design chair. “Our program prepares them to bring a clear point of view, strong craft, and an understanding of people to the complex opportunities ahead.”

Student work by Julia Hummel. Photography courtesy of the School of Visual Arts (SVA).

Building on SVA’s reputation as a leader in design education, the new MFA design degree is a two-year, multidisciplinary graduate program for designers looking to create meaningful change across industries in products, services, and more. With a powerful tagline, “Design What the World Needs Next,” this degree combines the school’s four graduate-level design programs (Design, Interaction Design, Products of Design, and Design for Social Innovation) into one interconnected degree built for a new era of design.

“Design has always been one of the cornerstones of SVA’s cultural contributions,” Hunt explains. “This next chapter is about preparing designers not only to respond to the world as it changes, but to shape it through rigorous practice, collaboration, critical thinking, experimentation, and meaningful connection to industry and society.”

Photography courtesy of the School of Visual Arts (SVA).

Launching next fall, MFA Design will be based at 136 W 21st Street in the heart of New York City’s bustling Chelsea neighborhood. Led by Randy Hunt, the program features studios, seminars, workshops, as well as critiques, collaborations, and networking opportunities with design professionals—plus access to communal studio spaces, a fabrication and coding lab, and flexible learning spaces. With a curriculum based on the intersection of critical inquiry and practical application, students are asked to research, prototype, develop, and test work that is culturally relevant and resonant.

“SVA’s design programs have always been shaped by working practitioners,” SVA President Christopher Cyphers says. “Our students learn from people who are actively defining the field. The opportunity now is to make those connections even more visible, more integrated, and more powerful across the graduate design experience.”

Photography by ANDREA MIRANDA SALAS & LORENA ESTRELLA (MFA 2020 DSI), courtesy of the School of Visual Arts (SVA).

Grounded in deep industry engagement and SVA’s broader cultural involvement in the city, this multidisciplinary degree underscores the importance of a design education that teaches real-world skills while also setting students up to become creative movers and shakers. Designers don’t just make objects or build buildings; they shape the world we live in.

Submit your application today to join the 2027 cohort here. Recruitment for the class of 2029 MFA Design candidates begins this fall.

#9194. Getty to help conserve art-filled 17th-century church in Peruvian Andes

Members of the local community in the Church of Rondocan Photo: Alejandra Velez, © 2026 J. Paul Getty Trust

An art-filled 17th-century church in the Andes mountains will soon begin five years of conservation work. The project will strengthen the building and preserve its collection of 330 historical objects—including eight paintings by the artist Bernardo Bitti (1548-1610), an Italian Jesuit priest who introduced Mannerism to the Viceroyalty of Peru in the 16th century.

Getty will work with the Peruvian Ministry of Culture to conserve the Church of Santo Tomás de Aquino, also known as the Church of Rondocan—named for the town in the Cusco region where it was built. The project will include seismic stabilisation using local materials; located 3,400m above sea level, the 340-sq.-m church is in an area prone to earthquakes.

“We provide all the advanced conservation techniques available, and we handle the structural design of the project,” Claudia Cancino, a principal project specialist at the Getty Conservation Institute (GCI), tells The Art Newspaper. The Peruvian government will finance the work, which will cost $5m and start in 2027. Like other churches in the Andean highlands, Rondocan has adobe walls (1.2m thick), buttresses and a wooden truss roof.

“The project is not only about the temple and its walls. It’s about the cultural and spiritual heritage of the church,” says César Ccorimanya Mayta, the parish priest at Rondocan for the past 17 years.

The Church of Rondocan and its surrounding landscape Photo: Luigi Barazzetti © 2026 J. Paul Getty Trust

Involving the community as caretakers of the temple is part of the conservation process. Cancino and her team completed a similar project at the Church of Santiago Apóstol in the nearby town of Kuñotambo in 2019. As part of that initiative, they showed locals how best to take care of the building—including deceptively simple tasks, like cleaning the floors.

“You have to understand how to sweep the church and with what, because if you stir up too much dust it sticks to the murals,” Cancino says. “All this training was done with the community of Kuñotambo. We even have a manual in Quechua,” the local Indigenous language.

Through the work in Kuñotambo, the GCI became familiar with the Church of Rondocan. “The community asked for our support so that they could request the Archdiocese of Cusco and the Ministry of Culture to work on their church,” Cancino says.

Technical examination and assessment of a painting from the series Principales Misterios de la Vida y Muerte de Cristo Nuestro Salvador y la Virgen Santísima, attributed to Bernardo Bitti © 2024 J. Paul Getty Trust

“This church is much more than a historic building. It is part of the community’s memory, identity and everyday life,” Fernando López Sánchez, Peru’s vice minister of cultural heritage, said in a statement.

As part of the conservation project, a Bitti painting will travel to Los Angeles for scientific analysis and conservation on the Getty campus.

Bitti arrived in Peru in 1575, creating paintings for churches in Lima and Cusco. When the Jesuits were expelled from the Americas by the Spanish Crown in 1767, their works were sold. It is believed that the parish priest at Rondocan at that time bought Bitti’s paintings in Cusco and had them transferred to the church. The discovery, less than two decades ago, of the only complete series of eight Bitti canvases has sparked renewed interest in the study of his work.

In addition to the paintings, the church’s collection includes sculptures from the viceroyalty era, manuscripts and silver liturgical objects. “The art collection in this small town in the middle of nowhere is breathtaking,” Cancino says.

#9193. How Mannington Commercial Approaches Design as a System

Family-owned flooring manufacturer Mannington Commercial aims to solve problems for interior designers and their clients. That’s why the company focuses on giving designers more freedom and flexibility with product, as discussed in The Art of Versatility last year. Building on that concept, Mannington Commercial designs products in families so individual flooring collections work together across an entire project.

“An entryway has different demands than a lobby, patient room, corridor, or collaborative area, but those spaces still need to feel connected. If every collection lives on its own island, then the designer has to create all of those relationships,” says Stacey Gerbman, Mannington Commercial Director of Design. “The shift is from thinking only about individual launches to thinking about the life of the entire portfolio.”

Rather than creating matching sets, Mannington Commercial establishes a design language that allows products to complement one another and carry a design concept throughout a project. Each new product should be distinct yet work with existing and future collections, simplifying specification for interior designers.

Stepping Stones. Photo courtesy of Mannington Commercial.

Mannington Commercial’s design team plans ahead to ensure new collections pair naturally with existing lines. “Before a collection is fully developed, we look at the portfolio as a whole: where there are gaps, which colors and undertones are important, what scales are missing, and which materials the new collection is likely to sit beside,” says Gerbman. The team considers how a collection might work with carpet, LVT, sheet, rubber, or an entryway product, as well as how scale and color should transition between materials.

For Mannington Commercial, the key to connecting carpet with LVT and other materials is its yarn system, which Gerbman describes as “color architecture.” A core palette of solids and twists provides a foundation that carries across collections while allowing for different effects. “We do not look at carpet in isolation,” Gerbman notes. “We place the poms and tufted trials next to LVT, sheet, rubber, and other materials and study undertone, value, temperature, and contrast.” Rather than seeking exact color matches, the goal is a “believable relationship.” Gerbman adds, “The hard surface may provide clarity and structure, while the carpet adds softness, depth, and variation. When the yarn bank is built thoughtfully, those materials can play different roles and still feel as if they belong in the same environment.”

Curated Underfoot. Photo courtesy of Mannington Commercial.

Curated Underfoot puts this approach into practice with Mannington Commercial’s first system of carpet and LVT for commercial interiors. Five neutral tones carry across the LVT and five carpet patterns, creating a shared color foundation. “But each surface and pattern brings a different level of texture and movement,” Gerbman explains. “A designer can stay tonal or create contrast through pattern and scale, and the result still feels connected without looking overly matched. It supports the system while leaving room for the designer’s own authorship.”

“Curated Underfoot reflects the way designers think about a space as a complete environment rather than a series of individual flooring decisions,” says Whitney LeGate, Senior Vice President, Commercial Product. “By bringing carpet and LVT together through one synchronized collection, we’re making it easier to create interiors that are visually cohesive and built to perform.”

Atto, a terrazzo-inspired LVT, anchors the system with bold pattern, layered movement and contemporary color that translates to carpet for a seamless transition between hard- and soft-surface flooring.

Stepping Stones. Photo courtesy of Mannington Commercial.

Another product family, Stepping Stones, combines performance and aesthetics in an LVT collection for healthcare settings. Six curated palettes pair complementary colors and textures across wood, stone, and other material expressions, with tonal terrazzo anchoring each palette. Patterns inspired by nature take on softer, warmer qualities to promote a serene, restorative environment. The palettes simplify specification and help designers maintain visual continuity throughout a healthcare facility, where arrival, waiting, treatment and recovery areas require different flooring but should still feel connected.

BioSpec. Photo courtesy of Mannington Commercial.

Mannington Commercial also makes BioSpec, a line of homogeneous sheet vinyl designed for high-use commercial and healthcare spaces. Mannington Commercial is the only manufacturer producing homogeneous resilient sheet vinyl in the United States. And it’s the only one making heterogeneous sheet vinyl in 6-foot, 9-foot, and 12-foot widths for easier installation, fewer seams, and less waste. Similar to the relationships in other product families, this line includes three variations tailored to specific needs: BioSpec Armor for demanding, high-traffic environments; BioSpec SR for enhanced slip resistance; and BioSpec MD for superior abrasion resistance and an extensive color selection. The products work together and pair with other Mannington Commercial resilient flooring and carpet.

LayeredLogic. Photo courtesy of Mannington Commercial.

Continuing this systems-based approach in 2027, Mannington Commercial is launching LayeredLogic, a heterogeneous sheet collection for healthcare interiors. Its three patterns share a visual language, allowing them to be layered, as the prints progress from subtle texture to more expressive designs. Created for acute care facilities, LayeredLogic gives designers a way to define spaces and create rhythm through an intentional palette designed to last and work with current and future Mannington Commercial LVT and carpet collections. By designing individual products to work together as part of a larger system, Mannington Commercial takes an approach that feels familiar and fitting for a family-owned company.

#9192. Monopoly and Scrabble Get a Scandinavian Modern Redesign

Monopoly and Scrabble have been fixtures of family game nights for generations, but their colorful boards and familiar pieces rarely stay out once the competition ends. When the last property has been traded or the final word spelled, everything usually disappears back into a cabinet. WS Game Company is rethinking that relationship between play and display.

The new Nordic Collection gives the two classic board games a Scandinavian-inspired redesign, replacing conventional folding boards and cardboard boxes with warm wood, understated graphics, and carefully considered details. Launched last month, the collection draws on the principles of Scandinavian modernism to create games that feel as much like design objects as they do as games.

“The Nordic Collection was inspired by the rich design history of Scandinavian modern design,” explains Kerry Addis, co-owner and COO of WS Game Company. She points to designers such as Hans Wegner and Arne Jacobsen, who combined natural materials and traditional craftsmanship with modern production techniques to create objects that were both innovative and inviting. For the Nordic Collection, the goal was to bring that same balance of familiarity and innovation to the games’ form, construction, and functionality.

The goal was to create something that could fit comfortably into an existing interior while offering meaningful innovations in form, construction, and practicality.

The most immediately noticeable change is the material palette. Both Monopoly Nordic and Scrabble Nordic feature wooden game boards made from individual panels that connect through concealed magnets. Instead of unfolding a conventional board, players snap the pieces together, creating a sturdy playing surface that breaks down for compact storage.

The assembly itself was designed to be as satisfying as the finished product. “The intuitive magnetic connections allow the user to snap the panels easily together, creating a solution that is as elegant and functional as it is satisfying to use,” explains James Fuschetti, WS Game Company’s senior industrial designer. Cork backing adds warmth while helping prevent the boards from sliding during a game.

Working with manufacturing partners, the designers selected woods and stains that would produce a warm tone with a subtle luster. Generously rounded corners on the storage boxes and other components soften their appearance while making them more comfortable to handle.

The result is a collection designed to complement a range of interiors rather than compete with them. Each game comes in a coordinating beechwood box that can sit comfortably on a shelf or coffee table, with the components stored neatly inside.

Each game comes in a coordinating beechwood box that keeps the components neatly organized while allowing the games to remain on display between uses.

Beyond the wooden construction, smaller details reveal how WS Game Company balanced Scandinavian influences with the visual identities of two instantly recognizable games.

In Monopoly Nordic, the traditional houses have become miniature pine trees. Instead of placing four houses side by side on a property, players stack them vertically to create increasingly tall conifers. As the game progresses, the board begins to resemble a Scandinavian forest.

The graphic design draws on the region’s history, too. Monopoly’s Chance and Community Chest cards have been recolored light blue and red, a subtle nod to early Swedish editions of the game. The railroad icon has been reimagined as an electric trolley, while the custom money takes cues from modernist Scandinavian banknotes, pairing crisp graphics with patterns inspired by traditional folk art.

Despite these updates, the game retains its recognizable corner-square icons, Chance question mark, and classic playing tokens, including the top hat and shoe. A wooden banker’s tray, die-cast tokens, and custom property deeds round out the set.

Scrabble Nordic takes a similarly considered approach. Its scorepad features graphics inspired by Scandinavian banknotes and folk art, while wooden letter tiles and racks bring warmth to the familiar game. The set also includes a microsuede tile bag, a pencil, and a sand timer with wooden end caps.

The designers were careful to preserve the details that make Scrabble instantly recognizable, from the size and weight of the letter tiles to the small triangular markings along the edges of premium squares. Those markings help players identify bonus spaces even when tiles cover the board, preserving a small but important functional detail of the original design.

Together, the two editions demonstrate how familiar games can be updated through materials, graphics, and playful details without losing the elements that make them enjoyable in the first place.

The collection builds on an idea WS Game Company has explored for years: Board games can be part of a home’s décor rather than hidden away between uses.

Its Vintage Bookshelf Collection takes a similar approach, packaging classic games in formats intended to blend into a bookshelf. The Nordic Collection extends that thinking through natural materials, a more sculptural presentation, and an emphasis on the physical experience of playing.

“We’ve always believed that good design should have staying power,” Addis says. Rather than chasing fleeting trends, the company aims to create products that can evolve with people’s interiors and remain relevant as their lives change.

As more daily activities migrate to screens, WS Game Company sees an opportunity to bring analog experiences back into everyday life. “Board games are a natural fit, bringing people together for shared experiences,” Addis says.

The Nordic Collection makes a case for finding new possibilities in objects we already know. Monopoly and Scrabble don’t need to be reinvented to feel fresh. Sometimes, a thoughtful change in materials, a more intuitive construction, or a miniature forest of wooden houses is enough to make a familiar game worth leaving out long after everyone has gone home.

#9191. EBBA Architects transforms former agricultural barn in Cornwall into a "calm sanctuary"

Photography by Rikard Kahn and Benni Allan

London studio EBBA Architects has updated and extended a house within a converted barn in Cornwall, stripping away previous alterations to create open, pared-back interiors.

Topped by a distinctive gambrel roof, the former agricultural barn had already been converted into a dwelling, but also undergone years of incremental, ill-suited adaptations and extensions.

EBBA Architects looked to restore the Dutch barn‘s original, open spatial character, expanding its area by almost a third with the addition of a pavilion-like extension that is framed by columns of white stone.

“The overall concept was about finding clarity in the form of the building and finding ways to add in a way that didn’t take away from the original character,” EBBA’s founding director, Benni Allan told Dezeen.

“Over the years the barn had gathered a series of piecemeal alterations that took away from the original simplicity. Our process involved removing later additions and then adding where felt most appropriate,” he added.

“The house is a place that will act as a place to enjoy the vast contrast of weather throughout the year, while also providing a calm sanctuary and background for family life.”

The ground-floor plan of Dutch Barn is based on the central position of an existing stair, around which a bathroom and storage core has been built to separate the more open kitchen and living spaces.

A row of full-height openings links the existing barn to its extension, where a long, uninterrupted space containing a skylit dining area and lounge opens out onto a covered colonnade via sliding doors.

“The intention is for the house to be used by the large family, and for there to be a blend between spaces,” Allan explained.

“We are always interested in making flexible arrangements in planform, to accommodate different ways of living.”

The home’s interior finishes were also guided by ideas of simplification, with plaster walls, concrete floors and gridded white-painted timber ceilings.

EBBA Architects wanted to emphasise material junctions, as seen in a new oak column in the kitchen, which has been rotated to highlight where it meets the flitch plates that connect it to the exposed ceiling beams.

Externally, this theme was extended into the design of the extension’s roof, which stops short of the edge of the stone columns to emphasise the point where the two meet.

The existing barn was clad in reused cedar shingles that were replaced where necessary, while the extension was built using white stone masonry that references the walls on the adjacent street.

“At first glance the house presents itself as a simple barn, but we like that a series of quite serious architectural moves have been complemented with some playful elements, such as the exaggeration of the junctions and the contrast between textured columns and clear, almost gallery-like floors,” explained Allan.

“We wanted the projecting roof and new columns to read as an independent object that reaches out into the garden and takes up the change in level, rather than as a continuation of the barn,” he added.

EBBA Architects has previously completed a cafe in Marylebone with clay plaster walls and an illuminated glass ceiling, and an apartment in London for its founder that is lined with Douglas fir.

Photography by Rikard Kahn and Benni Allan

#9190. Danny Kaplan and Vince Patti Expand Their Delf Furniture Collection

Delf began as a single bed. Danny Kaplan designed the Paravent Bed for his own home, basing its strong, paneled silhouette on the hinged screens of Jean-Michel Frank, before he and Vince Patti of Lesser Miracle saw the potential for a larger commercial collection. That collection launched in 2024. Following its commercial success, the two New York–based designers have expanded it with Delf II, adding a desk, a coffee table, a console, and a nightstand that extend the series beyond the bedroom.

The relationship between wood and ceramic remains central to the collection. Each piece is crafted from white oak and accented with hand-built ceramic, the pairing that defined the original bed and inspired the collection’s name. Delf derives from delven, the Dutch verb meaning to mine or to dig, a reference to the channels carved into the wood and filled by hand with ceramic tile inlays.

Kaplan, a self-taught ceramicist who founded his studio in 2015, creates the tilework, drawing inspiration from the pottery of Vallauris, a region in southern France known for its ceramics. It is offered in the studio’s signature glazes: Stone, Anthracite, Terrasig, Ivy, Lapis, Agate, Bronze, and Chestnut, along with a new Navy. Around the tile, the oak takes modernist architectural forms softened by rounded edges and subtle curves.

Bringing the two materials together requires a carefully sequenced production process. The ceramic components are fired separately, then individually fitted into the hand-built wooden structures. The drawer hardware is first modeled in clay, then cast in brass and aluminum. A single piece in the collection takes weeks to produce.

As with the original collection, the design process begins with Kaplan’s hand sketches before moving through drawing, discussion, prototyping, and digital modeling between the two studios.

For Kaplan, the expansion was an opportunity to explore how the original design language could translate to different furniture forms. The new pieces allowed the pair to continue “developing that language while thinking about how the collection could live throughout an entire interior.”

Patti sees the expansion as a natural evolution of their collaboration. The Brooklyn-based designer, whose practice draws on 1970s pulp fantasy, Timurid architecture, and the work of Frank Lloyd Wright, says the new collection “builds on the same principles as the original pieces, but with greater confidence and complexity.”

Leo Lei is the founder and editor of Leibal, a publication dedicated to minimalist design, architecture, and interiors. Through his writing and curatorial eye, he highlights thoughtful contemporary work from around the world.

#9189. Your Prototype Is Not Being Honest With Your Users (And Here’s How To Fix It)

Eric is a Creative Technologist at ProtoPie, where he pushes the boundaries of no-code prototyping. With a background in FinTech UX design, he brings firsthand … More about Eric ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at ProtoPie who help users turn their ideas into highly interactive animations and prototypes for mobile, desktop, web, and IoT. Thank you!

There’s a moment in almost every usability session where a participant pauses at the login screen, types something, and glances up: checking whether they’re “doing it right.” That pause is a clear sign. They’ve already clocked that this isn’t a real app, and every data point collected after that moment is filtered through that awareness.

In financial product testing, the problem is sharper. Finance users are trained to notice when something feels off: a balance that doesn’t add up, a field that accepts anything. When a banking prototype skips real authentication, participants don’t just disengage; they stop mid-session to flag it. The team walks away with findings that reflect how users behave in a demonstration, not in a real product.

The fix is narrower than you’d think. Identify the moment where participant trust is established and make that interaction real. In a banking app, that moment is the login.

This tutorial builds it: credentials that validate, a live error state, and a biometric animation that feels native — no code required.

The login flow, built around Pie Bank, a mobile banking prototype, includes functional text inputs, a masked password field, credential validation, a live error state, and a Face ID animation timed to feel indistinguishable from iOS.

In Figma, open the ProtoPie plugin with your login frame selected and choose Scene when exporting. Flattened collapses everything into a single image; Scene preserves your layer hierarchy so every element arrives in ProtoPie as a separate, targetable layer.

Before moving on: rename every layer meaningfully. “Input Username” not “Rectangle 14”. You’ll reference these names in formulas: vague names compound into real time lost.

ProtoPie’s native Input layer accepts real keyboard entry: participants type actual text, not tap a placeholder. Go to Text  → Input, drag an Input layer onto your canvas, and nest it inside your username field group. Match it visually: placeholder text Username, background fill and font to match your design.

Hit preview. Click the field. Type. That’s the prototype starting to behave like an app rather than depicting one.

Rename this layer Input Username, duplicate it, and nest the copy inside your password field group.

On the duplicated layer, change placeholder text to Password and set Type to Text Password. ProtoPie handles the masking: no custom logic needed.

Preview both fields: username shows text, password shows dots. It already feels real, and you haven’t written a single condition.

Add a new scene, even a blank one. The most common sequencing mistake in ProtoPie is trying to wire a navigation response before a destination exists. Create it first.

Select Log In, add a Tap trigger, set response to Jump, target your dashboard scene, transition Slide in from right to left.

Preview and tap. It navigates: but for any input, including nothing. The prototype is still lying. The next two steps are the fix.

At the bottom-left of ProtoPie, add two Text type variables: username and password. Bind each to its input layer with a formula:

Enable the debug icons: green overlays will show live variable values as you type. When you see your keystrokes appear in real time, the binding is confirmed.

Go back to the Tap trigger on the login button. Add a Condition with two rules, both must be true:

Move the Jump response inside this condition. Wrong credentials, empty fields, wrong format: none get through. Participants now have to actually log in. That single constraint changes the texture of every test session that follows.

Find your error message layer, rename it Error Text, set initial opacity to 0. Add a second condition (the inverse of the first), and inside it, a Change Property response setting Error Text opacity to 100.

Wrong credentials: error appears. Correct credentials: dashboard. Two outcomes: which is what makes this testable, not just demonstrable.

Go to Media, drag a Lottie layer onto canvas, load your Face ID file, and position it off-screen above the iPhone frame. On your Login with Face ID button, add a Tap trigger (rename it Tap Face ID) with four responses in sequence:

Without delays, all four responses fire at once and the scene jumps before the animation plays. Add offsets:

Enable Reset selected scenes on Jump: without it, navigating back leaves the animation stuck at Y: 60.

Preview: tap Face ID, animation drops in, plays, screen transitions. A biometric login indistinguishable from the real thing.

When authentication actually works, the error state becomes a genuine research touchpoint: do users understand the message, do they retry, do they reach for Face ID instead? These are questions a faked login can’t answer.

In stakeholder reviews, the flow speaks for itself. In engineering handoff, the interaction panel documents the behavior (conditional logic, variable bindings, timing) so engineers see intent, not interpretation.

This is why FinTech teams invest in login fidelity even when the login isn’t the feature being tested. It’s where participant trust is established. Get it right, and everything downstream produces better signal.

This tutorial is part of the FinTech Prototyping with ProtoPie series on the ProtoPie blog. The series builds Pie Bank from the ground up across four chapters, covering the dashboard, money transfer logic, and camera integration. If this tutorial was useful, the rest of the series goes further.

#9188. Reviving an Enduring Emblem of Simplicity, Loll Designs Launches the Here and There Collection

The best designs almost always come out of necessity and quiet observation. In the 1940s, legendary ecologist Aldo Leopold constructed a remarkably straightforward wooden bench so that he could sit outside his Wisconsin farmstead and contemplate nature’s primal force; the fundamental need for its conservation. The back-slanted seat was constructed from readily available dimensional lumber and almost immediately presented itself as an act of unpretentious, serendipitous genius: the quick assembly of a functional furnishing devised for a specific need but ultimately, one with universal potential. The particular brilliance of the design was its x-shaped self-bracing geometry, zero waste configuration, and uncomplicated assembly.

“Anyone that’s handy with a saw and some fasteners and lumber could easily build an Aldo bench,” says Eric Swanson, president of Duluth-based outdoor furniture brand Loll Designs. “That’s the beauty of it.” The Minnesota manufacturer recently teamed up with Michigan industrial design studio Argenta Park to turn the foundational artifact into the Here and There Collection. Named for Leopold’s belief that our appreciation for the natural world should balance between what’s nearby and farther afield, the cohesive and complementary suite of furnishings includes a dining chair, dining table, and of course, a bench.

This contemporary reinterpretation was twelve years in the making. For his outdoor wedding in 2014, Argenta Park designer Ricky Biddle was faced with the same practical challenge Leopold surmounted decades earlier: creating sturdy, durable, and comfortable outdoor seating. He didn’t want to rent generic, flimsy event furniture, so he spent his bachelor party assembling rudimentary Aldo benches. It was almost as if influential Italian designer Enzo Mari had sanctioned the task as one of his open-source “Autoprogettazione” self designs.

The pieces have remained a fixture of Biddle and his family’s everyday life ever since. This permanence prompted him to reconsider how its raw genius might be retooled using advanced manufacturing, elevated ergonomics, and year-round durability. He brought the idea to Argenta Park founder Churu Yun and the Loll Designs engineering team.

The best type of historical preservation is the kind that implements the latest technologies and refined strategies; doesn’t focus on creating replicas merely out of nostalgic reverence. “Not all historical designs lend themselves to being evolved into a modern-day furniture piece,” says Brian King, Loll Designs Brand and Marketing Director. “It’s more about being hyper selective in a design that has meaning, history, or a deep-rooted memory and identifying what’s most valuable.” Loll had done this many times before, most notably by bringing the ubiquitous Adirondack Chair up to contemporary standards.

While still carrying the original design’s understated silhouette, the re-edited and expanded collection carefully addressed the physical limitations of simple timber construction. Softly contoured surfaces replace flat planks, streamlined fastener assembly, and the use of 100% recyclable high-density polyethylene (HDPE)—available in Black, Charcoal Grey, Fog, and Sage—simplifies ongoing maintenance.

This calculus responds to changing demands: contemporary homeowners are increasingly looking for low-maintenance solutions that can withstand harsh seasonal shifts without sacrificing aesthetic refinement or tactile comfort. “With historical designs comes historical maintenance and poor ergonomics,” Swanson adds. “People want to enjoy their time outdoors sitting in their furniture more than working on it, which is why using alternative materials to traditional wood is a benefit; why a curved seat and backrest is so important; and why the right proportions—the height of the dining table—make all the difference.”

Leopold is widely considered the founder of wildlife ecology and his bench stands testament to that; allowing people to enjoy nature for as long as they want. The new Here and There Collection carries on that legacy.

#9187. The Big Review: Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous ★★★★½

“The Met’s prize Jackon Pollock”, Autumn Rhythm: Number 30 (1950), flanked by a pair of Lee Krasner’s collage paintings, Blue Level (1955, left) and Stretched Yellow (1955) Photo: Anna-Marie Kellen; courtesy Metropolitan Museum of Art

He was Jack the Dripper. She was The Wife. That is how it went for artist couples in gender-coded mid-century America (and elsewhere). Yet, Lee Krasner (1908-84) played more than a supporting role in her decade-long marriage to Jackson Pollock (1912-56). When his work eclipsed hers, she remained as committed to her own painting as she was to every aspect of his life—except his infidelity and the alcoholism that in 1956 drove him to his death. Even then, she put her devotion to consequential use in securing his legacy. Now the time has come to fully appreciate hers.

That is the organising principle behind Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous, the gorgeous and largely convincing blockbuster at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. While other US museums have previously surveyed the artists separately and in tandem, for the Met curators David Breslin and Brinda Kumar, none gave Krasner, a first-generation Abstract Expressionist, a fair shake.

Their exhibition strives to give a primacy to Krasner’s work that parallels Pollock’s. Note whose name comes first in the show’s title. Its subtitle likewise derives from a Krasner at the she-who-laughs-last finale. What’s more, a dramatically lit, black box of a gallery starts it off with a bracing presentation of six vertical abstractions that Krasner made in the 1950s by collaging cuttings from her unsold paintings with pieces of canvas and bits of Pollock’s drawings punctuated by slashes of pink and orange.

Nonetheless, the eye keeps moving to a window-like opening that functions as a proscenium for the theatre of Pollock’s Convergence: No. 10 (1952), an immense and riveting painting of black paint skeins shot with explosions of colour. Mounted on an angled, freestanding wall in another room, the sight offers viewers a taste of what is in store: signature Pollocks ricocheting off shape-shifting Krasners, and vice-versa.

If only the curators did not show Krasner still riding his coattails. Pollock’s name remains the bigger draw. Ultimately, he still comes off as the bigger trailblazer, and she, his foremost champion, more willing to risk failure to experiment and invent. As Breslin speculated during the press preview: “I don’t think we would have a Jackson Pollock if it weren’t for what Krasner did to support his work.”

There is no way to test that theory, but if Krasner and Pollock proves anything, it is that the artists’ relationship was so codependent that the reverse may be just as true. Yet, today her influence and market value pale before his. Krasner’s auction record, set at Sotheby’s in 2019, is $11.7m for The Eye is the First Circle (1960), one of her larger canvases in the show. That is not chump change, but this year Christie’s sold Pollock’s Number 7A (1948) for $181.2m, an eye-watering price but still short of the reported $200m that financier Ken Griffin paid David Geffen, in 2016, for Number 17A (also 1948).

Photo by Anna-Marie Kellen; courtesy of The Met

Krasner and Pollock met in 1942, when she was better-known to the Abstract Expressionist crowd in New York and Pollock the only unfamiliar name in a show of American and European Modernists (partially recreated at the Met) that the painter John Graham organised and included works by both. By linking their small, vibrant abstractions with works by Pablo Picasso, Joan Miró, Henri Matisse, Amadeo Modigliani, Giorgio de Chirico and Willem de Kooning, the show virtually jumpstarted their careers. It also made them a couple.

Krasner introduced herself in a spontaneous visit to Pollock’s studio and was so dazzled that she hit a creative block. That did not stop them from dating. He was a Midwestern former student of Thomas Hart Benton in thrall to Picasso and Mexican muralists. She was inspired by Arshile Gorky’s abstractions and Matisse’s cut-outs. Soon he was importing a Matissean palette to his painting and showing at Peggy Guggenheim’s Art of this Century gallery. Sales were not brisk. Pollock’s drinking was more prodigious. Krasner insisted they marry and move to Springs, in East Hampton—to protect him from himself—and persuaded Guggenheim to cover the downpayment.

Relocating did the trick for three unusually sober years—long enough for Pollock to produce his breakthrough drip paintings and achieve lasting fame, before settling, intermittently, into new bouts of alcoholism and depression; a creative paralysis set in. Krasner’s career took off, with a confident 1955 solo show at New York’s Stable Gallery.

Breslin and Kumar take care not to place the artists’ works close together, so Krasner’s modestly-scaled paintings can hook the eye without being overwhelmed by Pollock’s volatile monumentalism. Until she was widowed and took over Pollock’s now-famous barn, Krasner worked in their kitchen and he in an upstairs bedroom. Two contiguous galleries, both painted black, approximate the size of the artists’ studios and distill the show’s thesis with luminous economy, leading viewers from the lyrical, early choreography of his pours, drips and stains to her smaller but exquisite Little Images—mosaic-like geometries painted with a palette knife.

From these sepulchral chambers the show opens to a large, high-ceilinged gallery flooded with daylight from newly revealed windows on Central Park. Here, Convergence hangs, backed with the Met’s prize Pollock, Autumn Rhythm: Number 30 (1950). The operatic shift in tone and scale drives home the outsize renown Pollock achieved after a 1949 feature in Life magazine posed the question, “Jackson Pollock: Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?”

In the same gallery, tellingly, the eight collage paintings Krasner showed at Stable Gallery turn from the Pollocks to face each other like the stones of Stonehenge and look just as ritualistic, if more elated. After that, it’s back to black for a segment titled Re:Echo (after a Krasner), where Pollock’s arabesque, later works hang near her Robert Motherwell-like abstractions of the same period.

The rest of the show is all Krasner, but she outlived Pollock by 28 years. The swirling, abstracted floral landscapes became monumental, but appear in a few too many galleries, homogenizing their visual impact. The point—that no full understanding of one artist can come without the other—has already been made, capped by the one side-by-side juxtaposition: The Deep (1953), a chilling canvas where Pollock nearly obliterated a dark biomorph in clouds of white, and Birth (1956), an image of interlocking pink and black forms that Krasner painted the year he died. That pairing said it all.

Will this show correct a historic imbalance? Probably not market-wise, but a reputational correction seems both necessary and likely.

Installation view including Pollock's The Deep (1953)and Krasner's Birth (1956) in Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous

Photo by Anna-Marie Kellen; courtesy of The Met

The New York Times’s Holland Cotter describes the exhibition as an “exercise of art-historical reset”, and calls its installation of Pollocks “an entrancing sight”, while exulting in the “distinctive impression of personal joy” in Krasner’s post-Pollock work. In The Wall Street Journal, Karen Wilkin applauds the curators for encouraging “concentration on their work, rather than the mythology attached to both painters”, and on her Instagram, Jasper Johns’s biographer Deborah Solomon raves: “It’s like holding two opposed thoughts in your brain at the same time and wondering if your head will explode from the exhilaration of it all.”

#9186. Algorithmic Theming Engines: Building Self-Correcting Color Systems With `contrast-color()`

Durgesh Rajubhai Pawar is a freelance developer dedicated to building high-performance, accessible web applications. He specializes in orchestrating complex … More about Durgesh ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

The HTTP Archive Web Almanac has been tracking color contrast failures for years. The numbers have barely moved. After half a decade of design system tooling, accessibility linters, and entire JavaScript libraries dedicated to computing readable text colors, 70% of websites still fail basic WCAG contrast checks in 2025. The WebAIM Million paints an even grimmer picture — 83.9% of homepages flagged for low contrast text in 2026, up from 79.1% in 2025. The rate improves by maybe a few percentage points per year on one benchmark and actually gets worse on another. That’s not progress — that’s proof that relying on runtime JavaScript for something this fundamental doesn’t scale across the open web. We didn’t need better libraries. We’ve needed better CSS.

The contrast-color() function is that better CSS. One declaration. The browser runs the contrast math during style computation, before the page paints, and hands you the right text color. No library, no build step, no hydration flash.

Note: If you’ve seen it called color-contrast() in older articles and spec drafts — that name was changed, and the old syntax no longer works in any browser.

The Level 5 version is simple. You give it a color. It gives you back black or white, whichever has more contrast against your input.

Change --brand-color to neon green, text goes black. Change it to midnight navy, text goes white. Swap themes at runtime via JavaScript and the text adapts instantly — no event listeners, no recalculation.

A few things to know about the current version:

Meet Smashing Workshops on front-end, design & UX, with practical takeaways, live sessions, video recordings and a friendly Q&A. With Brad Frost, Stéph Walter and so many others.

This function lives across two specifications. That’s unusual and worth understanding.

CSS Color Level 5 defines what browsers ship today. One color in, black or white out. The algorithm is deliberately marked “UA-defined”, meaning the browser decides what math to use internally. Right now, every engine uses WCAG 2.x relative luminance. But that “UA-defined” label isn’t accidental — it’s a planned escape hatch.

You’ll see APCA (Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm) mentioned a lot in this context. APCA models how human eyes actually perceive contrast, factoring in font weight, spatial frequency, and ambient light — a genuine improvement over the WCAG 2.x formula. By not locking “use WCAG 2.x” into the Level 5 spec, browser vendors could swap to APCA later without breaking any existing code. If the spec had shipped with a wcag2() keyword as the default, every site using it would’ve been stuck on the old math permanently.

But APCA’s future is far less certain than the hype suggests. Adrian Roselli’s “WCAG3 Contrast as of April 2026” lays out the current situation clearly: APCA was pulled from the WCAG 3 working draft in mid-2023 after failing to gain enough Working Group support. The WCAG 3 spec currently says the contrast algorithm is “yet to be determined,” and the standard itself may not be finalized until 2030 or later. Roselli also filed a Chromium issue in May 2024 asking for the “Advanced Perceptual Contrast Algorithm” experiment flag to be removed from DevTools entirely, arguing that the implementation is outdated and risks misleading developers into thinking APCA is further along — or more official — than it actually is. That issue is still open.

None of this means APCA is dead. The research behind it is peer-reviewed and substantive, and its creator has noted that colors passing APCA guidelines greatly exceed WCAG 2 minimums in the vast majority of cases. But right now, there is no guarantee APCA will be the algorithm that replaces WCAG 2.x — and that uncertainty matters for contrast-color(). If a different algorithm wins out, or if WCAG 3 adopts something entirely new, the “UA-defined” label means browsers can adapt without breaking your code. It also means the Level 6 features — candidate color lists, target ratios, the tbd-fg/tbd-bg keywords — are all designed around an algorithm that may or may not materialize in its current form.

CSS Color Level 6 adds the extended syntax — candidate color lists and target contrast ratios:

The browser would evaluate each candidate left to right and pick the first that meets the 4.5:1 AA threshold. The tbd-fg and tbd-bg keywords indicate whether the base color is foreground or background, which matters for directional contrast models like APCA. This is all Working Draft territory — doubly so given APCA’s uncertain status. Use the Level 5 version for now.

This one’s in better shape than most new CSS features. All three major engines have shipped it in stable releases: Chrome 147 (April 2026), Firefox 146, and Safari 26.0. It reached Baseline Newly Available status in April 2026. Check caniuse for the full version matrix. All three engines pass the Web Platform Tests for contrast-color(), which means the edge cases (e.g., tie-breaking logic, color space conversion, syntax parsing) behave the same across browsers.

The raw global support percentage on caniuse looks low, but that mostly reflects enterprise browsers and people who never update. If you’re reading this, your browser almost certainly supports it already.

Progressive enhancement is straightforward using @supports:

Older browsers get white text with a dark shadow for legibility. Supporting browsers get the native calculation. Nobody sees broken text.

One thing to watch for: automated accessibility scanners (Lighthouse, Axe, etc.) can’t evaluate text-shadow. They only look at the computed color against background-color. So the fallback will still get flagged as a contrast failure in CI/CD pipelines, even if the shadow makes the text perfectly legible to human eyes. If your team runs automated a11y checks, you may need to allowlist that specific rule or add a comment explaining why the flag is a false positive.

This can trip people up: “I used the contrast function, so my site passes accessibility checks now, right?”

Mathematically? Usually yes. There is a persistent myth that for certain “mid-tone” backgrounds, both black and white fail the standard WCAG 4.5:1 AA ratio. That’s mathematically false. Under the WCAG 2.x relative luminance formula, there is absolutely no background color where both pure black and pure white fail AA. One (or both) will always pass.

Take #2277d3 (a medium blue). It sits right on a mathematical knife-edge where both black and white actually pass AA (both hit roughly 4.58:1). contrast-color() will hand you whichever has the slight mathematical edge.

But here is the actual gotcha: the WCAG 2.x math has known perceptual blind spots. That same #2277d3 with black text mathematically passes AA, but to human eyes, it can be incredibly difficult to read. contrast-color() gives you mathematical compliance, which is great for automated audits, but that doesn’t always equal perceptual accessibility. (This is exactly why APCA exists and why the spec was designed to let browsers swap algorithms later.)

Furthermore, if you’re aiming for the stricter WCAG AAA standard (7.0:1), a true dead zone does exist. For backgrounds with a luminance between roughly 10% and 30%, neither black nor white will hit 7:1. In those cases, contrast-color() can’t save you — it just hands you the “least bad” failing option.

If you’re animating a background from white to black on hover:

The background fades smoothly over one second. But because the Level 5 output is a discrete value (black or white), the text color can’t be interpolated. It snaps.

And here is the visual gotcha: the snap doesn’t happen halfway through. If you’ve been building themes for a while, you probably have muscle memory from the old Sass days, where we checked if lightness($bg) > 50%. That relied on HSL lightness, where 50% is the geometric midpoint.

But WCAG 2.x relative luminance is a non-linear scale. Under the WCAG formula, the mathematical tipping point — where black and white have identical contrast against the background — actually occurs at approximately 18% relative luminance (specifically ~17.9%).

Because of that, the visual behavior during a white-to-black fade is heavily skewed. The text doesn’t snap in the middle. It stays black for the vast majority of the animation, only snapping to white at the very tail-end of the transition when the background gets extremely dark. It’s a jarring, late hard cut.

You might assume transition-behavior: allow-discrete fixes this. It doesn’t. allow-discrete does not fix the jarring visual experience because it cannot interpolate a binary output; it only shifts the timing of the hard snap to the 50% mark of the animation duration. If you need smooth text color transitions, you’ll have to layer color-mix() or manage the crossfade yourself.

If the background is a perfect middle gray where both black and white produce identical contrast ratios, the spec has a hardcoded tiebreaker: white wins. Not a big deal in practice, but worth knowing if you’re debugging gray palettes and the text isn’t doing what you expect.

The function takes a flat value. You can’t pass it a gradient or a url(). contrast-color(linear-gradient(...)) is a parse error. If your background is a photo or a complex gradient, you still need JavaScript or manually color-pick for overlay text.

Pass a semi-transparent color, and the browser blends it against an assumed opaque canvas (usually white) before running the contrast math. It’s not ignoring your alpha channel — it’s compositing it. But the result might surprise you if you expected the function to “see through” to whatever’s actually behind the element.

If a user enables Windows High Contrast, the forced-colors: active media query kicks in and the browser aggressively overwrites author-defined colors. contrast-color() bows out — forced system colors like CanvasText take over completely. You don’t need to write manual media queries to undo your contrast logic; the browser handles the hierarchy.

Black or white sounds limiting, but once you feed that output into other CSS color functions, you can build an entire component palette off a single custom property.

Pure black text on a vibrant card looks fine. Pure white on a coral card can feel flat. What if the contrast text was a very dark or very light tint of the background color instead?

Kevin Hamer explored related territory in his CSS-Tricks piece “Approximating contrast-color() With Other CSS Features”, where he used OKLCH lightness and round() to approximate the black/white switch without contrast-color() — essentially oklch(from round(1.21 - l) 0 0). That’s a polyfill strategy: get the binary light/dark decision working in browsers that don’t support the native function yet. What we’re doing here is different — we start with contrast-color()’s native output and then enrich it by injecting the background’s own hue:

When contrast-color() returns white, l is 1 (full lightness). When it returns black, l is 0. By pulling the background’s hue back in and adding a touch of chroma, you get text that reads as a deep dark indigo or a pale icy indigo instead of generic black/white. Hamer’s approach gives you the black/white decision without browser support; this one takes the decision the browser already made and gives it personality.

Fair warning: By tweaking the lightness and chroma of the black/white output, you can push a borderline contrast ratio into failing territory. Always run your tinted output through an accessibility linter before shipping.

Also worth noting: This example chains two very modern features — contrast-color() and oklch(from ...). If either one isn’t supported, the entire declaration fails silently. Your @supports block needs to test for both:

Similar idea, simpler API. Mix the sharp black/white output back into the background to soften it:

One custom property driving text, border, and potentially box-shadow or outline. Change --alert-color and the entire component recalculates.

This pattern also works well for ::placeholder text, which is a common pain point in dynamic theming. Placeholder text should be readable but visually softer than the input’s main text — color-mix() with contrast-color() gets you there:

50% mix gives you a muted but legible placeholder that adapts automatically to whatever background the input sits on.

For apps that support system light/dark mode:

When the operating system switches to dark mode, --surface resolves to #121212, and contrast-color() returns white. No media queries, no JavaScript theme detection. The whole chain resolves natively.

The practical payoff: every one of these libraries existed because CSS couldn’t do contrast math. If you’re only using them for readable-text-color selection, you can pull them out of your runtime entirely:

You might still need these for generating complex color scales, but the contrast-for-readability use case is now covered natively.

Beyond bundle size, there’s a performance angle that’s easy to overlook. Those JavaScript libraries don’t just cost you network bytes — they run on the main thread. Every time a theme changes or a component mounts with a dynamic background, your JS has to parse the color, compute luminance, decide black or white, and write the result back to the DOM. That’s main-thread work competing with layout, event handlers, and everything else your app is doing. contrast-color() moves all of that into the browser’s native style computation phase — heavily optimized C++ that runs before paint. For apps with lots of themed components, that’s a real difference in responsiveness.

There’s also a subtle bug that goes away: hydration flash. In React or Vue SSR apps, the server renders HTML without JavaScript. The client then hydrates, running JS to calculate contrast and inject the correct text color. For a brief window between initial paint and hydration, the text is either invisible or the wrong color. Moving contrast into CSS eliminates that entirely — the browser resolves the correct color during the initial paint, before JavaScript loads.

Sass era. You’d write a function that checked lightness($bg) > 50% and returned black or white at compile time. Worked for static themes. Completely useless for user-picked colors, CMS palettes, or dark mode, because the output was baked into the CSS file and could never change at runtime.

The variable toggle hack. When CSS custom properties shipped, people got creative. GitHub used a version of this for their issue label picker — splitting colors into --r, --g, --b channels, calculating Rec.709 luminance inside calc(), multiplying by negative infinity, and clamping to 0 or 1. It worked. It was also unreadable, unmaintainable, and would break silently if you got one parenthesis wrong. (Kevin Hamer’s OKLCH-based approximation is the most elegant version of this lineage — cleaner math, better perceptual alignment — but it’s still a workaround for a function that now ships natively.)

contrast-color() replaces all of these approaches with a single function call. And because the spec lets browsers upgrade the underlying algorithm, your code won’t need to change if and when a successor to WCAG 2.x contrast math lands — whether that’s APCA or something else entirely.

That 70% failure rate was never about developers refusing to care about contrast. It was about the distance between caring and shipping — the library, the build step, the runtime calculation, the hydration flash, the one component someone forgot to wire up. Every gap in that chain was a spot where accessibility quietly dropped out.

contrast-color() doesn’t make developers care more. It makes caring cost nothing.

#9185. The Best Gifts Under $100 for Design Enthusiasts

A $100 budget opens up plenty of possibilities for thoughtful gifting, especially when you know where to look. It’s enough to find something genuinely well-designed, whether that’s a sculptural object for the home, an everyday essential with an unexpected twist, or a small indulgence someone might not think to buy for themselves.

The trick is finding gifts that offer something beyond their price tag. We’re drawn to pieces with a distinctive point of view, clever functionality, and materials or details that make them memorable. With that in mind, we’ve rounded up our favorite gifts under $100, from playful accessories and colorful tabletop finds to practical objects that make everyday routines a little more interesting.

Le Creuset brings a little holiday magic to its classic cocotte with an embossed Christmas tree lid and a gold-finished star knob. Crafted from durable glazed stoneware, the 24-ounce vessel moves easily from oven to table, making it ideal for individual pot pies, baked pasta, or warm desserts. Available in six colors, it’s a festive gift that’s just as practical as it is charming.

The Noël Mini Cocotte is available at williams-sonoma.com for $62.

Inspired by the pleated designs of Issey Miyake, Wooj’s Kinoko Lamp borrows the delicate look of folded paper without its fragility. Each mushroom-shaped shade is 3D printed from recycled plastic in Brooklyn, creating an accordion-like texture that softly diffuses light. Available in Amber, Smoke, Olive Oil, and Natural, it’s a small but striking addition to a desk, bookshelf, or bedside table.

The Kinoko Lamp is available at wooj.design for $95.

With its puffy, quilted silhouette and compact proportions, Calpak’s Luka Mini Duffel brings a playful edge to an everyday essential. The lightweight, water-resistant bag packs plenty of functionality into its design, including padded shoulder straps, dedicated bottle pockets, and a luggage sleeve with a hidden security compartment. Available in 18 colors, from understated neutrals to shimmering metallics, it’s a practical gift with plenty of personality.

The Luka Mini Duffel is available in select colors at calpaktravel.com for $98.

Chess has always been a game of strategy, but Printworks makes a case for keeping the board on display between matches. This contemporary take on the classic features wooden playing pieces, a sleek acrylic-topped board, and a coordinated storage box designed to look at home on a coffee table. Available in multiple colorways, it’s a gift that brings people together while doubling as decor.

The Classic Chess Set is available at printworksmarket.com for $79.

A little whimsy goes a long way when it comes to travel accessories. Antler’s Heritage Leather Aeroplane AirTag Holder takes the shape of a miniature airplane, crafted from scratch-resistant green leather with subtle stitched details. A discreet compartment keeps an Apple AirTag securely tucked away, while a leather lanyard attaches easily to luggage or a favorite travel bag. It’s a charming way to keep track of belongings without sacrificing style.

The Heritage Leather Aeroplane AirTag Holder is available at ⁠antler.com for $75.

Belgian jewelry designers Wouters & Hendrix bring a touch of surrealism to the tabletop with this trio of sculptural candleholders. Inspired by 1920s surrealist art, the hand-painted stoneware pieces combine graphic checkerboard patterns, contrasting colors, and three playful silhouettes. Arrange them together for an unexpected centerpiece or scatter them around a room for little moments of visual interest.

The Les Objets Mouleversants Candle Holder Set is available at lumens.com for $85.30.

Photography courtesy of Present & Correct

Originally created as teaching tools for Spanish classrooms, these solid beechwood geometric shapes have been in production since 1934. The 15-piece set comes in a wooden box with a hinged lid, inviting recipients to explore form, proportion, and composition through hands-on experimentation. Part educational tool, part sculptural desk accessory, it’s an unexpected gift for anyone fascinated by architecture, mathematics, or design.

The Wood Polyhedra Set is available at presentandcorrect.com in two sizes: large box ($82) and small box ($41).

What happens when a cardboard prototype becomes the finished product? Dutch designer Annebet Philips brings her playful, sketch-like aesthetic to this porcelain teapot, preserving the uneven edges and fold lines of the original cardboard model. Hand-painted black outlines give it an almost cartoonish quality, turning an everyday kitchen essential into a conversation piece.

The Carte Blanche Teapot is available at lumens.com for $98.

Designed with birds’ feeding habits in mind, this sculptural feeder takes its cues from traditional grain silos. Its cylindrical form accommodates birds that cling vertically while eating, while a clever filling mechanism helps keep seeds clean and dry. Made from upcycled plastic, the Finnish design comes in three earthy colors and brings a modern touch to outdoor spaces.

The Silo Bird Feeder is available at goodeeworld.com for $75.

Disguised as colorful coffee table books, Printworks’ jewelry boxes bring a little personality to everyday organization. Cloth-covered exteriors feature bold typography and playful color combinations, while padded interiors keep rings, earrings, necklaces, and other treasures neatly arranged. Available in a range of designs and sizes, they’re made to be displayed rather than tucked away in a drawer.

The Jewelry Boxes are available at printworksmarket.com starting at $49.

Inspired by traditional French bedside drinkware, Maison Balzac’s colorful glass carafe turns a practical necessity into a small design moment. The matching cup sits neatly over the opening when not in use, creating a sculptural silhouette that’s equally at home on a nightstand or desk. Made from dishwasher-safe borosilicate glass, the set comes in six colors and can even double as a vase.

The Bedside Carafe is available at comingsoonnewyork.com for $90.

German artist Marc David Spengler brings his graffiti-inspired compositions to the sofa with this colorful collaboration for Slowdown Studio. Playful abstract shapes give the 20-inch cotton pillow cover an artistic quality, while a soft, neutral reverse offers a quieter alternative. It’s a thoughtful gift for someone who appreciates original artwork in unexpected places. Pillow insert sold separately.

The Bessie Throw Pillow Cover is available at slowdownstudio.com for $80.

A rolling pin might not seem like an exciting gift, but this one makes a convincing case otherwise. Handcrafted in Tennessee from black walnut, cherry, and maple, East Fork’s Mixed Wood Rolling Pin celebrates the natural beauty of contrasting hardwoods. Its tapered, French-style silhouette offers greater control when working dough, while the substantial construction makes it a kitchen tool designed to last for years.

The Mixed Wood Rolling Pin is available at eastfork.com for $98.

Photography courtesy of Sophie Lou Jacobsen

Designer Sophie Lou Jacobsen transforms an everyday tabletop essential into a set of four gleaming spirals, sand-cast in aluminum and finished with nickel plating. Their fluid, looping forms bring a playful graphic element to the table, whether they’re holding drinks or arranged together as decorative objects. It’s a perfect gift for anyone who appreciates design in the smallest details.

The Spiral Coaster Set is available at sophieloujacobsen.com for $85.

With its undulating silhouette and bold blue-and-white palette, this ceramic vase brings a sense of movement to an otherwise stationary object. Standing nearly 12 inches tall, its sculptural curves make an impression with or without flowers, while the narrow opening is well suited to a few carefully chosen stems. It’s a playful addition to a shelf, mantel, or dining table.

The Ceramic Swish Vase is available at anthropologie.com for $58.

The number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy. Before you spend a dollar on a website, business cards, or inventory, you need to validate that real people will pay real money for what you are offering.

Validation does not require a perfect product. It requires proof of demand. Talk to 10 people who match your target customer. Describe what you plan to offer. Ask two questions: "Would you pay for this?" and "How much would you pay?" If 3 or more say yes with a specific dollar amount, you have a viable idea. If most say "that sounds cool" but hesitate on paying, you have a hobby.

The FI community has a particular advantage here. Many FI seekers have already cut their expenses to the point where a side business does not need to generate massive revenue to make a meaningful impact. Even $500 to $1,000 per month in side business income — invested consistently — can shave years off your FI timeline.

Forget building a $1 million business. Your only goal is reaching $1,000 in total revenue as quickly as possible. That first $1,000 proves three things: people will pay you, you can deliver, and the business model works. Everything after $1,000 is optimization. The FI community calls this the "ramen profitable" stage — your business covers its own costs and generates even a small surplus. From there, you compound both your skills and your revenue.

Side business income is the ultimate FI accelerator because it attacks both sides of the equation. Your day job covers expenses while 100% of your side income goes directly to investments. If your side business generates $1,500 per month and you invest all of it at 7% annual returns, you will have over $450,000 in 15 years. That is not a theoretical number — that is the real math of why thousands of FI seekers build side businesses.

One of the first decisions you face is how to structure your business legally. For most side businesses, the choice is between operating as a sole proprietorship (the default — no paperwork needed) or forming an LLC (Limited Liability Company). Here is the honest comparison.

A sole proprietorship is what you are by default when you start earning money on the side. There is no registration required at the federal level (though you may need a local business license). The income flows directly to your personal tax return on Schedule C. The downside: your personal assets — savings, home equity, investments — are not separated from business liabilities.

An LLC creates a legal separation between you and your business. If someone sues your business, your personal assets are generally protected. Formation costs range from $50 (states like Kentucky and Colorado) to $500 (California charges $800 per year just for the privilege of having an LLC). For most side businesses, an LLC is worth forming once you have paying customers.

Side business income is taxed differently than your W-2 paycheck, and the surprises can be painful if you are not prepared.

Self-employment tax: You pay both the employee AND employer portions of Social Security and Medicare — a combined 15.3% on top of your income tax. On W-2 income, your employer covers half. On side business income, you cover it all.

Quarterly estimated taxes: The IRS expects you to pay taxes as you earn, not once a year in April. If you owe more than $1,000 in taxes from side business income, you need to file quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040-ES) by April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.

Deductions that reduce your tax bill: Home office (simplified method: $5/sq ft up to 300 sq ft = $1,500 deduction), internet (business percentage), equipment, software subscriptions, mileage ($0.76 per mile in 2026), health insurance premiums (if self-employed), and retirement contributions (Solo 401k allows up to $72,000/year). These deductions are a significant FI advantage because they reduce both income tax AND self-employment tax.
